source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 4 (PDF 75-92, printed 72-89); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 4 (Work, Energy and Power), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.
4.1 Work done by a constant force

blocks.prompt: 1 In Physics, the term work involves:
blocks.explanation: In Physics, work involves two things: force and displacement (4.1).

book_ref.quote: the term work involves two things (i) force, and (ii) displacement

blocks.prompt: 2 When a constant force F displaces an object through d in its own direction, the work done is:
blocks.explanation: Work is the product of the magnitudes of the force and the displacement, W = Fd (Eq. 4.1).

book_ref.quote: work W is defined as the product of the magnitude of the force F and magnitude of the displacement d

blocks.prompt: 3 A man pushes hard against a wall that does not move. The work done on the wall is:
blocks.explanation: If the displacement is zero, no work is done even if a large force is applied, as in pushing a wall (4.1).

book_ref.quote: if displacement is zero, no work is done even if a large force is applied

blocks.prompt: 4 If a force F makes an angle θ with the displacement d, the work done is:
blocks.explanation: Only the component F cos θ along the displacement does work, so W = (F cos θ)d = Fd cos θ (Eq. 4.2).

book_ref.quote: the work done is equal to the product of the component of force along the direction of the displacement

blocks.prompt: 5 Work is written as W = F⃗·d⃗. This shows that work is:
blocks.explanation: W is the scalar (dot) product of F⃗ and d⃗, so work is a scalar quantity (Eq. 4.3).

book_ref.quote: Equation (4.3) shows that work is a scalar quantity.

blocks.prompt: 6 One joule is equal to:
blocks.explanation: From W = Fd, the SI unit of work is N m, known as joule: 1 J = 1 N m (4.1).

book_ref.quote: SI unit of work is N m known as joule (J).

blocks.prompt: 7 Work done by a force is positive when the angle θ between force and displacement is:
blocks.explanation: If θ < 90°, work is done and it is positive work (4.1).

book_ref.quote: If θ < 90°, work is done and it is said to be positive work.

blocks.prompt: 8 A force acts on a moving body perpendicular to its displacement. The work done by this force is:
blocks.explanation: If θ = 90°, cos θ = 0, so no work is done (4.1).

book_ref.quote: If θ = 90°, no work is done.

blocks.prompt: 9 The work done by a force on a body is negative when the angle between force and displacement is:
blocks.explanation: If θ > 90°, cos θ is negative and the work done is negative (4.1).

book_ref.quote: If θ > 90°, the work done is said to be negative.

blocks.prompt: 10 A constant force of 25 N moves a box 8 m in the direction of the force. The work done is:

book_ref.quote: The force displaces the object through a displacement d in the direction of force.

blocks.prompt: 11 A rope pulls a trolley with a force of 40 N at 60° to the displacement. The work done in moving it 5 m is:

book_ref.quote: If the force F makes an angle θ with the displacement d

blocks.prompt: 12 A force of 50 N acts at 30° to the displacement and moves a body 12 m. The work done is about:

book_ref.quote: where the rope pulls at an angle θ to the displacement d

blocks.prompt: 13 A force of 8 N acts on a body while it moves 5 m, and the work done by the force is −40 J. The angle between the force and the displacement is:
blocks.explanation: cos θ = W/(Fd) = −40/(8 × 5) = −1, so θ = 180°; work is negative because θ > 90° (4.1).

book_ref.quote: From the definition of work, we find that:

blocks.prompt: 14 A frictional force of 15 N acts opposite to the motion of a block while it slides 4 m. The work done by friction is:

book_ref.quote: If θ > 90°, the work done is said to be negative.

blocks.prompt: 15 For a constant force, the work done is represented on a force-displacement graph by:

options.text: the intercept on the force axis
the length of the graph line

blocks.explanation: The shaded area under the force-displacement graph equals Fd, the work done (Fig. 4.4).

book_ref.quote: the area under a force-displacement curve can be taken as to represent the work done by the constant force

blocks.prompt: 16 A constant force of 12 N acts on a body in the direction of motion from d = 0 to d = 3 m. The area under its force-displacement graph is:
blocks.explanation: The graph is a horizontal line; the rectangle's area = 12 N × 3 m = 36 J, which is the work done (4.1).

book_ref.quote: As the force does not vary, in this case, the graph will be a horizontal straight line.

blocks.prompt: 17 If the force is not along the displacement, the graph used to find work is plotted between:
blocks.explanation: When F is not along d, the graph is plotted between F cos θ and d (4.1).

book_ref.quote: In case the force F is not in the direction of displacement, the graph is plotted between F cos θ and d.

blocks.text: 4.2 Work done by a variable force

blocks.prompt: 18 As a rocket moves away from the Earth, the force of gravity on it varies:

options.text: directly as the distance from the Earth's centre
as the inverse square of the distance from the Earth's centre
as the square of the distance

blocks.explanation: Gravity varies as the inverse square of the distance from the Earth's centre, so it is a variable force (4.2).

book_ref.quote: as a rocket moves away from the Earth, work is done against the force of gravity

blocks.prompt: 19 Which is an example of a variable force given in the chapter?

options.text: The weight of a book resting on a table
A steady pull of fixed size on a rope
A force that stays the same at every point
The force exerted by a spring as it is stretched

blocks.explanation: The force exerted by a spring increases with the amount of stretch, so it varies (4.2).

book_ref.quote: the force exerted by a spring increases with the amount of stretch

blocks.prompt: 20 To find the work done by a variable force, the path is divided into short intervals because during each small interval the force is:
blocks.explanation: During each small interval the force is taken as approximately constant, so ΔW = F cos θ Δd for it (4.2).

book_ref.quote: During each small interval, the force is supposed to be approximately constant.

blocks.prompt: 21 The total work done by a variable force is found by:

options.text: adding the work done in all the small intervals
multiplying the largest force by the total displacement
averaging only the first and last forces
dividing the force by the displacement

blocks.explanation: W_total = ΔW₁ + ΔW₂ + … + ΔWₙ = Σ Fᵢ cos θᵢ Δdᵢ (Eq. 4.4).

book_ref.quote: The total work done in moving the object can be calculated by adding all these terms.

blocks.prompt: 22 In finding the work of a variable force as a sum of rectangles, the result becomes more accurate when:

options.text: the intervals Δd are made larger
the intervals Δd are made very small
only the first rectangle is used

blocks.explanation: Sub-dividing into a large number of intervals so that each Δd becomes very small makes Eq. 4.4 more accurate; as Δd → 0 the result is exact (Eq. 4.5).

book_ref.quote: If we sub-divide the distance into a large number of intervals so that each Δd becomes very small

blocks.prompt: 23 The work done by a variable force between two points P and Q equals:

options.text: the slope of the F cos θ versus d curve
the product of the forces at P and Q
the area under the F cos θ versus d curve between P and Q
the length of the curve from P to Q

blocks.explanation: Work by a variable force equals the area under the F cos θ versus d curve between P and Q (Fig. 4.7).

book_ref.quote: the work done by a variable force in moving a particle between two points is equal to the area under the F cos θ verses d curve

blocks.prompt: 24 A force stays at 8 N from d = 0 to d = 3 m and then falls uniformly to zero at d = 7 m. The work done from d = 0 to d = 7 m is:
blocks.explanation: Rectangle: 8 N × 3 m = 24 J; triangle: ½ × 4 m × 8 N = 16 J; total = 40 J (area under the curve, 4.2).

book_ref.quote: The work done by the force is equal to the total area under the curve from d = 0 to d = 6 m.

blocks.prompt: 25 A force increases uniformly from 0 to 10 N while a body moves from d = 0 to d = 4 m along the force. The work done is:
blocks.explanation: The area under the line is a triangle: ½ × 4 m × 10 N = 20 J (4.2).

book_ref.quote: Thus, the work done given by Eq. 4.4 equals the sum of the areas of all the rectangles.

blocks.prompt: 26 The space around the Earth in which its gravitational force acts on a body is called:
blocks.explanation: This space is called the gravitational field (4.3).

book_ref.quote: The space around the Earth in which its gravitational force acts on a body is called the gravitational field.

blocks.prompt: 27 When a ball falls downward, the work done on it by the gravitational force is:
blocks.explanation: The displacement is in the direction of the gravitational force, so the work is positive (4.3).

book_ref.quote: If displacement is in the direction of gravitational force, the work is positive.

blocks.prompt: 28 When a body is lifted upward, the work done on it by the gravitational force is:
blocks.explanation: The displacement is against the gravitational force, so the work done by gravity is negative (4.3).

book_ref.quote: If the displacement is against the gravitational force, the work is said to be negative.

blocks.prompt: 29 When a body is moved along a horizontal path in the gravitational field, the work done by gravity is zero because:

options.text: the weight mg is parallel to the path
the body has no mass along a horizontal path
the weight mg is perpendicular to the path

blocks.explanation: Along a horizontal path such as AD, mg is perpendicular to the displacement, so the work is zero (4.3).

book_ref.quote: The work done along AD is zero, because the weight mg is perpendicular to this path

blocks.prompt: 30 A 2 kg body is moved from the ground to a point 3 m higher, once straight up and once along a long curved path. The work done by gravity along the curved path is:

options.text: −58.8 J, the same as straight up

blocks.explanation: Work by gravity is independent of the path: W = −mgh = −2 × 9.8 × 3 = −58.8 J along both paths (4.3).

book_ref.quote: the work done by the gravitational force does not depend on the choice of the path

blocks.prompt: 31 To find the work done by gravity along a curved path, the path is imagined as a series of:
blocks.explanation: The curved path is broken into horizontal and vertical steps; work is done only along the vertical steps (Fig. 4.10).

book_ref.quote: Imagine the curved path to be broken down into a series of horizontal and vertical steps

blocks.prompt: 32 Which statement about the work done by the gravitational force is correct?

options.text: It is greater along a longer path
It is zero along every path
It is independent of the path followed
It depends on the speed of the body

blocks.explanation: Work done by the gravitational force is independent of the path followed (4.3).

book_ref.quote: Work done by gravitational force is independent of the path followed.

blocks.prompt: 33 A body is carried from A up to B and brought back to A. The total work done by gravity on it is:
blocks.explanation: Going up gives −mgh and coming down gives +mgh; along a closed path the work by gravity is zero (4.3).

book_ref.quote: Can you prove that the work done, along a closed path, such as ACBA or ADBA (Fig. 4.9), by the gravitational force is zero?

blocks.prompt: 34 A force is called conservative if the work done by it:

options.text: is never zero in a closed path
is independent of the path, or is zero in a closed path

blocks.explanation: A force is conservative if its work between two points is independent of the path, or its work in a closed path is zero (4.3).

book_ref.quote: If the work done by a force in moving an object between two points is independent of the path followed

blocks.prompt: 35 Which of the following is a conservative force?
blocks.explanation: Gravitational, electrostatic and elastic spring forces are conservative (4.3); friction, air resistance and rocket propulsion are non-conservative.

book_ref.quote: other examples of conservative force are electrostatic force and elastic spring force

blocks.prompt: 36 A force whose work between two points depends on the path of motion is called:
blocks.explanation: A force is non-conservative if its work depends on the path of motion (4.3).

book_ref.quote: A force is non-conservative if the work done by it in moving an object between two points or in a closed path depends on the path of motion.

blocks.prompt: 37 A block is pushed from P to Q against a kinetic friction of 5 N, once along a 6 m path and once along a 10 m path. The work done by friction along the two paths is:
blocks.explanation: Friction does negative work = friction × path length: −5 × 6 = −30 J and −5 × 10 = −50 J; the work depends on the path (4.3).

book_ref.quote: does negative work equal in magnitude to the frictional force multiplied by the length of the path

blocks.prompt: 38 A box is dragged around a closed path of length 8 m against a kinetic friction of 4 N. The total work done by friction is:
blocks.explanation: Friction does negative work along the whole path: −4 × 8 = −32 J; for a non-conservative force the work in a closed path is not zero (4.3).

book_ref.quote: Moreover, the total work done by a non-conservative force in a closed path is not zero.

blocks.prompt: 39 Which of the following is listed in the chapter as a non-conservative force?
blocks.explanation: Air resistance, tension in a string, normal force and rocket propulsion are non-conservative; the other three are conservative (4.3).

book_ref.quote: Other example of non-conservative force are air resistance, tension in a string, normal force and propulsion force of a rocket.

blocks.prompt: 40 Power is defined as:

options.text: the rate at which work is being done
the product of work and time

blocks.explanation: Power is the measure of the rate at which work is being done (4.4).

book_ref.quote: Power is the measure of the rate at which work is being done.

blocks.prompt: 41 If work ΔW is done in time Δt, the average power is:
blocks.explanation: P_av = ΔW/Δt (Eq. 4.6).

book_ref.quote: then the average power P_av during the interval Δt is defined as:

blocks.prompt: 42 The instantaneous power is the limit of ΔW/Δt as:
blocks.explanation: P = lim (Δt → 0) ΔW/Δt (Eq. 4.7).

book_ref.quote: If work is expressed as a function of time, the instantaneous power P at any instant is defined as:

blocks.prompt: 43 Power can also be written in terms of force F⃗ and velocity v⃗ as:
blocks.explanation: Since ΔW = F⃗·Δd⃗ and Δd⃗/Δt = v⃗, P = F⃗·v⃗ (Eq. 4.8).

book_ref.quote: where ΔW is the work done in short interval of time Δt.

blocks.prompt: 44 One watt is equal to:
blocks.explanation: The watt is one joule of work done in one second, 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹ (4.4).

book_ref.quote: The SI unit of power is watt, defined as one joule of work done in one second.

blocks.prompt: 45 In base units, the watt is:
blocks.explanation: 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹ = 1 kg m² s⁻² ÷ s = 1 kg m² s⁻³, as in Example 4.2 (4.4).

book_ref.quote: P = 7.7 × 10² kg m² s⁻³ = 7.7 × 10² W

blocks.prompt: 46 The kilowatt-hour is a unit of:
blocks.explanation: The kilowatt-hour is the commercial unit of electrical energy (4.4).

book_ref.quote: However, a commercial unit of electrical energy is kilowatt-hour.

blocks.prompt: 47 One kilowatt-hour is equal to:

book_ref.quote: One kilowatt- hour is the work done in one hour by an agency whose power is one kilowatt.

blocks.prompt: 48 A motor does 1800 J of work in one minute. Its average power is:

book_ref.quote: The rate, at which work is done, is often of interest in practical applications.

blocks.prompt: 49 A truck engine pushes the truck with a force of 500 N along its velocity of 20 m s⁻¹. The power delivered is:

book_ref.quote: In the definition of work, it is not clear, whether the same amount of work is done in one second or in one hour.

blocks.prompt: 50 A 2 kW heater runs for 3 hours. The energy it uses is:

book_ref.quote: Sometimes, for example, in the electrical measurements, the unit of work is expressed as watt second.

blocks.prompt: 51 A 60 kg girl runs up stairs of vertical height 6.0 m in 5.0 s. Her power output is about:

book_ref.quote: A 70 kg man runs up a long flight of stairs in 4.0 s.

blocks.prompt: 52 According to the table of approximate powers, which device has the largest power?
blocks.explanation: A jumbo jet's power is about 1.3 × 10⁸ W, far more than a car (1.1 × 10⁵ W) or a heater (2 × 10³ W) (4.4).

book_ref.quote: For Your Information: Approximate Powers

blocks.prompt: 53 The approximate power of a pocket calculator given in the chapter is:
blocks.explanation: The table gives a pocket calculator about 7.5 × 10⁻⁴ W; 1.5 W is a two-cell flash light and 120 W a coloured TV (4.4).

book_ref.quote: For Your Information: Approximate Powers

blocks.prompt: 54 About how much energy does a car use from petrol in its life time, according to the chapter?
blocks.explanation: It takes about 9 × 10⁹ J to make a car, and the car then uses about 1 × 10¹² J from petrol in its life time (4.4).

book_ref.quote: It takes about 9 × 10⁹ J of energy to make a car

blocks.prompt: 55 The energy of a body is its:
blocks.explanation: Energy of a body is its capacity to do work (4.5).

book_ref.quote: Energy of a body is its capacity to do work.

blocks.prompt: 56 The energy possessed by a body due to its motion is called:
blocks.explanation: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion (4.5).

book_ref.quote: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion

blocks.prompt: 57 A book placed on a high shelf has energy due to its changed position. This energy is:
blocks.explanation: Potential energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its changed position (4.5).

book_ref.quote: potential energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its changed position

blocks.prompt: 58 Kinetic energy and potential energy are both kinds of:
blocks.explanation: The kinetic energy and the potential energy both are kinds of mechanical energy (4.5).

book_ref.quote: The kinetic energy and the potential energy both are the kinds of mechanical energy.

blocks.prompt: 59 In deriving the formula for kinetic energy, the kinetic energy of a car whose engine is switched off is taken equal to:

options.text: the force of friction f only
the work done by its engine before switching off
the work fd it does against friction before stopping

blocks.explanation: The car does work fd against friction before stopping; this work, done due to its motion, is its kinetic energy (4.5).

book_ref.quote: The ability of a body to do work due to its motion is its kinetic energy.

blocks.prompt: 60 As the car slows down and stops, its acceleration is negative because:

options.text: it is produced by friction acting opposite to the motion

blocks.explanation: The acceleration is produced by the frictional force acting opposite to the direction of motion, so a = −f/m (4.5).

book_ref.quote: its acceleration a is negative because it is produced by force of friction f

blocks.prompt: 61 The SI unit of kinetic energy is:
blocks.explanation: Kinetic energy equals the work the body can do, so its unit is that of work, the joule (4.5).

book_ref.quote: Since, kinetic energy is equal to work which the body is capable of doing

blocks.prompt: 62 A 4 kg trolley moves at 5 m s⁻¹. Its kinetic energy is:

book_ref.quote: Let us derive a formula for the kinetic energy of a moving body.

blocks.prompt: 63 If the speed of a car is tripled, its kinetic energy becomes:
blocks.explanation: K.E. = ½mv² ∝ v², so tripling v makes K.E. 3² = 9 times (Eq. 4.9).

book_ref.quote: Consider a car running with a constant speed on a road.

blocks.prompt: 64 A body's mass is doubled and its speed is halved. Its kinetic energy becomes:
blocks.explanation: K.E. = ½mv²: new K.E. = ½(2m)(v/2)² = ½ × (½mv²), i.e. half (Eq. 4.9).

book_ref.quote: As long as it is moving, it is doing work against the force of friction of the road.

blocks.prompt: 65 A car of weight 9800 N moving at 10 m s⁻¹ is stopped by its brakes in 25 m. The average force of friction is (g = 9.8 m s⁻²):
blocks.explanation: m = w/g = 1000 kg; ½mv² = fd gives f = (½ × 1000 × 10²)/25 = 2000 N (as in Example 4.3).

book_ref.quote: Brakes are applied and it is brought to rest in a distance of 80 m.

blocks.prompt: 66 According to the table of approximate energy values, which has the smallest energy?

options.text: Fission of one atom of uranium
K.E. of a molecule of air
K.E. of a car at 90 km h⁻¹

blocks.explanation: The K.E. of an air molecule is about 6 × 10⁻²¹ J, smaller than uranium fission (1.8 × 10⁻¹¹ J) and the others (4.5).

book_ref.quote: For Your Information: Approximate Energy Values

blocks.prompt: 67 Potential energy is possessed by a body because of its:

options.text: position in a force field or its constrained state

blocks.explanation: Potential energy is due to position in a force field, e.g. the gravitational field, or due to a constrained state (4.5).

book_ref.quote: The potential energy is possessed by a body because of its position in a force field

blocks.prompt: 68 The energy stored in a compressed spring is called:
blocks.explanation: Energy stored in a compressed or stretched spring is elastic potential energy (4.5).

book_ref.quote: This form of energy is called the elastic potential energy.

blocks.prompt: 69 The relation P.E. = mgh is true only:

options.text: near the surface of the Earth
at infinite distance from the Earth

blocks.explanation: mgh is true only near the Earth's surface where the gravitational force is nearly constant (4.5).

book_ref.quote: which is true only near the surface of the Earth where the gravitational force is nearly constant

blocks.prompt: 70 A 5 kg box is raised 4 m near the Earth's surface. The gain in its potential energy is:

book_ref.quote: The relation for the calculation of the work done by the gravitational force or potential energy is mgh

blocks.prompt: 71 The absolute gravitational potential energy of an object at a position is the work done by the gravitational force in displacing it from that position to:
blocks.explanation: Absolute gravitational P.E. is the work done by gravity in displacing the object from that position to infinity, where gravity becomes zero (4.5).

book_ref.quote: is the work done by the gravitational force in displacing the object from that position to infinity

blocks.prompt: 72 In deriving the absolute P.E., r² = (r₁ + Δr/2)² is simplified to r₁r₂ because:

options.text: (Δr)² is very small compared with r₁² and is neglected

blocks.explanation: As (Δr)² << r₁², it is neglected: r² = r₁² + r₁Δr = r₁(r₁ + Δr) = r₁r₂ (4.5).

book_ref.quote: As (Δr)² << r₁², so (Δr)² can be neglected as compared to r₁².

blocks.prompt: 73 The absolute gravitational potential energy of a body of mass m at a distance r from the Earth's centre is:
blocks.explanation: U = −GMm/r, obtained by adding the work of all steps from r to infinity (4.5).

book_ref.quote: This is also known as the absolute value of gravitational potential energy of a body at a distance r from the centre of the Earth.

blocks.prompt: 74 The negative sign in the absolute potential energy U = −GMm/R shows that the Earth's gravitational field is:
blocks.explanation: The negative sign shows that the Earth's gravitational field for mass m is attractive (4.5).

book_ref.quote: The negative sign shows that the Earth's gravitational field for mass m is attractive.

blocks.prompt: 75 As a body is raised farther from the Earth's centre, its absolute potential energy U = −GMm/r:
blocks.explanation: When r increases, U becomes less negative, i.e. U increases, reaching zero at infinity (4.5).

book_ref.quote: Note that when r increases, U becomes less negative i.e., U increases.

blocks.prompt: 76 The work needed to take a body of mass m from the Earth's surface to infinity is:
blocks.explanation: U at the surface is −GMm/R and zero at infinity, so work GMm/R must be done on it (4.5).

book_ref.quote: if we want to raise the body up to infinite distance, we will have to do work on it equal to GMm/R

blocks.prompt: 77 A body has absolute potential energy −8.0 × 10⁹ J at the Earth's surface (r = R). At r = 2R its absolute potential energy is:
blocks.explanation: U ∝ −1/r, so doubling r halves U: −8.0 × 10⁹/2 = −4.0 × 10⁹ J (4.5).

book_ref.quote: Now the absolute potential energy on the surface of the Earth is found by putting r = R

blocks.prompt: 78 The initial velocity with which an object goes out of the Earth's gravitational field is called:
blocks.explanation: This is the escape velocity (4.6).

book_ref.quote: The initial velocity of an object with which it goes out of the Earth's gravitational field, is known as escape velocity.

blocks.prompt: 79 When the initial upward velocity of an object is increased (but below escape velocity), it:

options.text: rises to a greater height before coming back
comes back faster than it was thrown

blocks.explanation: With increased initial velocity the object rises higher before coming back (4.6).

book_ref.quote: With increased initial velocity, the object rises to the greater height before coming back.

blocks.prompt: 80 A body escapes the Earth's gravitational field when its initial kinetic energy equals:

options.text: the increase in P.E. from the surface to infinity, GMm/R

blocks.explanation: ½mv_esc² = GMm/R, the increase in P.E. from the surface to infinity (4.6).

book_ref.quote: The body will escape out of the gravitational field if the initial K.E. of the body is equal to increase in P.E.

blocks.prompt: 81 The escape velocity from the Earth's surface is given by:
blocks.explanation: v_esc = √(2GM/R) and GM/R = gR, so v_esc = √(2gR) (Eqs. 4.14, 4.15).

book_ref.quote: The escape velocity corresponds to the initial kinetic energy gained by the body

blocks.prompt: 82 The escape velocity v_esc = √(2GM/R) of a body does NOT depend on:
blocks.explanation: The mass m cancels in ½mv² = GMm/R; v_esc depends only on G, M and R (4.6).

book_ref.quote: where M and R are the mass and radius of the Earth respectively.

blocks.prompt: 83 The value of the escape velocity from the Earth is approximately:
blocks.explanation: v_esc comes out to be about 11 km s⁻¹ (the table gives 11.2 km s⁻¹) (4.6).

book_ref.quote: The value of v_esc comes out to be approximately 11 km s⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 84 From the table of escape speeds, which heavenly body has the smallest escape speed?
blocks.explanation: Moon 2.4 km s⁻¹ is the smallest; Mercury 4.3, Earth 11.2, Jupiter 61 km s⁻¹ (4.6).

book_ref.quote: For Your Information: Some Escape speeds (km s⁻¹)

blocks.prompt: 85 A planet has g = 4.0 m s⁻² at its surface and radius R = 2.0 × 10⁶ m. The escape velocity from it is:

book_ref.quote: It is our daily life experience that an object projected upward comes back to the ground

blocks.prompt: 86 If both g and R of a planet were four times as large, its escape velocity √(2gR) would become:
blocks.explanation: v_esc ∝ √(gR); gR becomes 16 times, so v_esc becomes √16 = 4 times (Eq. 4.15).

book_ref.quote: If we go on increasing the initial velocity of the object, a stage comes when it will not return to the ground.

blocks.prompt: 87 According to the work-energy theorem, the work done on an object by a net force equals:

options.text: the change in its kinetic energy

blocks.explanation: The change in kinetic energy of an object equals the work done on it by a net force (4.7).

book_ref.quote: The change in kinetic energy of an object is equal to the work done on it by a net force.

blocks.prompt: 88 In the derivation of the work-energy theorem, which equation of motion is used?
blocks.explanation: The acceleration is found from 2ad = vf² − vi², then compared with a = F/m to get Fd = ½mvf² − ½mvi² (4.7).

book_ref.quote: Whenever work is done on a body, it increases its energy.

blocks.prompt: 89 A 2 kg ball's speed increases from 3 m s⁻¹ to 7 m s⁻¹. The work done on it by the net force is:

book_ref.quote: This is also known as work-energy principle.

blocks.prompt: 90 A net force of 10 N acts on a 1 kg body at rest over a distance of 5 m. Its final speed is:
blocks.explanation: Fd = ½mvf²: 50 = ½ × 1 × vf², vf² = 100, vf = 10 m s⁻¹ (4.7).
